subject: Streaming & token-split follow-up — latency, concurrency, and implementation handoff
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.inference.com>

Cc: laura_bennett@redwood.inference.com, rishi_malhotra@redwood.inference.com
Date: Sun, 11 Oct 2026 09:12:04 -0700
Subject: Discovery recap: streaming + token-split tradeoffs and proposed handoff

Thanks for the productive call earlier — quick written recap and proposed next steps so we have a clear handoff to eng. TL;DR: your primary ask is sub-500ms perceived latency for streamed clinical summaries at p95 while supporting bursts up to 80 concurrent sessions. That combination pushes specific tradeoffs for context handling and partial-output flush design.

Key notes from today (what we heard):
- Typical user request: 1–2 short patient notes + 3–4 structured fields (~350–900 input tokens).
- Expected model output: brevity preferred, typical 120–600 output tokens (variable).
- Streaming requirement: client must render partial sentences as they arrive (incremental updates).
- SLO: target p95 end-to-end latency (time-to-first-token) = 350ms; p99 soft target = 650ms.
- Concurrency: steady-state 20–40 sessions, burst to 60–80 concurrent.
- Privacy: patient PHI requires no external telemetry; all inputs remain in Linq VPC.

Redwood implications / recommended mitigations:
- Token-split approach: break input -> short prompt prefix (static patient metadata) + dynamic prompt body. Cache KV for static prefix across requests for a session to avoid re-encoding.
- Partial flush vs full-token buffering: we can stream partial logits (token-by-token) but flushing smaller chunks increases overhead. Recommend a hybrid: flush after sentence boundaries or after ~32 tokens to amortize decoding cost.
- Batching lanes and concurrency isolation: dedicate low-latency lanes for streaming with small batch sizes (1–4) and a separate high-throughput lane for non-streaming/prediction jobs.
- Quantization/Model choice: suggest an 8-bit variant of a 13B model for a good latency/cost balance; 7B might reduce latency further but risks quality regressions on clinical language.
- Fallback: when low-latency lane is saturated, automatically route to a slightly cheaper model with graceful degrade (shorter max output) + client notice.

Requested deliverables from Linq by Oct 15:
1) Representative payloads (attached sample_payloads.csv) including worst-case input sizes and expected output ceilings.
2) Confirmation whether hallucination tolerance allows output truncation/fallback messaging.
3) Any redaction rules that must be applied server-side before streaming tokens.

Next steps (proposed schedule):
- Oct 15: Linq to drop sample payload CSV + any redaction rules into shared Drive.
- Oct 18 (30–60 min sync): Engineering deep-dive (Connor + Rishi + Linq eng) to run through prefix caching mechanics, streaming test harness, and concurrency lane config.
- Oct 23: Redwood to run a small perf matrix (p50/p95/p99) on representative payloads and share a short report.

Attachments: sample_payloads.csv (see included examples and a few worst-case rows).

Thanks — looping in Connor and Rishi for the technical handoff below.

—Marissa

- Confirmed numbers: steady 30 concurrent editors during clinic hours; spikes historically hit ~75 for release events.
- Output expectations: most summaries are short (120–250 tokens), but some care-path summaries can be ~600 tokens. We can't truncate clinical findings; shorter fallback messages are acceptable only for non-critical notes.

Looping in a slightly more technical reply to set expectations from the runtime side. Short bullets + implications: 

- Prefix KV caching: we can cache the key-value memory for the static prefix (patient metadata) per session. That will save ~30–60ms on first-token for repeated requests depending on prefix size. Cache eviction needs an LRU and a per-session TTL (we typically recommend 10–15 minutes).
- Tokenization and split costs: splitting inputs into multiple prompt parts requires re-tokenizing shared segments unless we maintain raw offsets. To avoid re-tokenization overhead, we prefer canonicalizing the prefix in a single cached token buffer.
- Partial flush tradeoffs: flushing every token increases per-token decode overhead ~8–15% compared to 32-token flushes because of more frequent context switching and network frames. However, perceived latency improves. We'll measure p95 time-to-first-byte vs p95 total decode time in the perf run.
- Batch sizes: low-latency lane should use micro-batches (1–3). That keeps jitter low. High-throughput lane can batch 8–16. Autoscaling rules will spin up more instances when queue depth exceeds a threshold.
- Concurrency lanes and cost: reserving capacity for low-latency lanes increases base cost; we can offset with a burstable design that borrows from general pool during off-peak.
- Streaming test harness: we'll want a small harness from Linq with a synthetic ramp to 80 concurrent sessions using your worst-case payload to measure p95 and tail.

Action items for Redwood eng (Connor/Rishi):
1) Run an initial latency matrix for the attached sample_payloads.csv and return p50/p95/p99 times for both token-flush=1, token-flush=32, token-flush=64.
2) Prototype KV prefix caching with a TTL and measure cache-hit delta on time-to-first-token.
3) Prepare a short demo (10–15 min) showing the UX difference between token-per-token and 32-token flushes.

I added a short design doc to the Drive link (see related_links) with a diagram of how streaming lanes and fallback routing would be implemented within Redwood.
